title: Annotated Song of Wasted Effort
author: Master Hanshan
excerpt: "Fei" means to spend time and energy; "xian" means useless, a waste of effort. Feixian means spending time and energy with no real result—what is commonly called doing useless work.

inline.s: The original text is taken from the Dream-Wanderings Collection
Appendix: The Life of Master Hanshan (Vernacular Version)
Fei" means to spend time and energy; "xian" means useless, a waste of effort. Feixian means spending time and energy with no real result—what is commonly called doing useless work.
In the Song of Wasted Effort, Master Hanshan points out the common pitfalls of wasted effort in cultivation and shows how to step out of them.

Take this passage, for example: "Preaching the Way is easy, realizing it is hard; unless stray thoughts are cleared, all effort is marred. When worldly dust and toil obstruct the mind, in mountain depths in stillness no peace you find." It states plainly that to preach the Way without realizing it oneself is like talking about food without eating one's fill. If one's own stray thoughts are not cleared, then preaching and realizing alike are wasted effort. But if

worldly toil and dust constantly obstruct the mind, then going off to sit in stillness in the deep mountains is of no use either. The overall meaning, therefore, is this: one must put down all ten thousand conditions, purify and clear away stray thoughts, realize the Way by practicing the Way, and only when one has truly awakened to the Way should one preach it—for only then is there real benefit for oneself and for others. In this way one steps out of the pitfall of preaching.

Preaching the Way is easy, realizing it is hard;
unless stray thoughts are cleared, all effort is marred.
When worldly dust and toil obstruct the mind,
in mountain depths in stillness no peace you find.

To preach the Way to others is easy; to realize it oneself is hard. Unless stray thoughts are cleared, all is idle (without clearing stray thoughts, all is wasted effort); when worldly dust and toil constantly obstruct the mind, going to the deep mountains to sit in stillness is futile as well.

[Realizing the Way] To practice the right Way in person and thereby awaken to it. To preach the Way while having no realization of it oneself, if one misleads students, brings great evil consequences upon others and oneself alike. [Always] All of it. [Always idle] All of it is useless. [In vain] To no purpose, futilely. For example: to expend spirit and strength in vain.

To leave home is easy; to observe the precepts and rules is hard. With no faith or vow at all, all is idle; to hold no pure precepts is labor spent for nothing—though one shaves one's head and leaves home, it is futile.

To cultivate is easy; to meet a teacher is hard. If one does not meet a clear teacher, all is idle; to be clever in one's own conceit is strength spent for nothing—blind and sightless cultivation is futile.

[If no clear teacher comes, all is idle] To "meet a clear teacher" means to cultivate in accordance with a clear teacher's instructions; it does not necessarily mean that a clear teacher must transmit the teaching to one in person. "If no clear teacher comes, all is idle" means that to practice blindly without following a clear teacher's instructions is wasted effort. For example, how one must recite the Buddha's name in order to be reborn in the Pure Land: Masters Tanluan, Daochuo and Shandao, together with the patriarchs and great masters of every generation, have all given specific and clear instructions, and to recite the Buddha's name in accordance with their instructions is to "meet a clear teacher." But to follow what false teachers say, or to cleverly improvise a method of one's own imagining—such as "to call the name is certainly to be reborn," "reciting with a scattered mind also certainly brings rebirth," "faith and vow alone certainly bring rebirth," "to believe is to be reborn"—that is to "not meet a clear teacher."

To be defiled by the six dusts is easy; to escape the entanglements of the six dusts is hard. If the afflictions are not cut off, all is idle; to court conditions with feeling and habit is strength spent for nothing—if the fruit of the Way is not attained, it is futile.

[The six dusts] The dust of form, the dust of sound, the dust of scent, the dust of flavor, the dust of touch, and the dust of mental objects. "Dust" means defilement: it can defile people's pure mind, so that the true nature cannot be revealed. They are also called the six objects, that is, the outer objects grasped by the six sense faculties. [Toils of dust] The mind toiling over dust-objects; another name for affliction. [To court conditions with feeling and habit] To scheme and contrive with the consciousness of feeling and habitual tendencies, while mistaking it for cultivation.

To hear the teachings is easy; to take them to heart and practice them is hard. To slight and scorn one's honored teacher, all is idle; to be proud and self-exalted is strength spent for nothing—though one's cleverness cover the world, it is futile.
[Self-exalted] To think oneself a cut above others.

To study the Way is easy; to awaken to the Way is hard. If one does not apply effort, all is idle; to be able to believe but not to practice is strength spent for nothing—empty talk and discussion are futile as well.

To shut the gate is easy, to keep the gate hard;
if you will not cultivate, all is marred.
The body in the cell, the mind outside the door—
a thousand years within will profit you no more.

To enter retreat is easy; to keep the retreat in earnest practice is hard. If one is unwilling to cultivate steadfastly, all is idle; with the body inside the cell and the mind outside it, a thousand years without leaving the retreat is futile as well.

To recite the Buddha's name is easy; a heart of true sincerity is hard. When mouth and mind disagree (the mind is not sincere: the mouth recites the Buddha's name while the mind thinks of other things), all is idle (all is wasted effort); to recite Amitābha Buddha with the mouth while the mind thinks of other things—though the throat be shouted hoarse, it is futile.

[Faith] A heart of true sincerity; when mouth and mind disagree, it is false. Hence the next line reads, "when mouth and mind disagree, all is idle (all is wasted effort)." The "faith" here is not the faith of faith, vow and practice, but means sincerity and trustworthiness.
For example, the "trustworthy wind" is the wind that, year after year, arrives on time as soon as a certain season comes—a wind of true reliability.

[True sincerity] Honest, not deceitful. [Though the throat be shouted hoarse, it is futile] Because "the mouth recites Amitābha while the mind is scattered" (reciting with a scattered mind) cannot accomplish the continuity of ten thoughts at the moment of death (this is the minimum requirement for rebirth in the Pure Land; for details see
), and so one is not reborn, and the effort is wasted.
Here Master Hanshan points out incisively:
"The mouth recites Amitābha while the mind is scattered
, though the throat be shouted hoarse, it is futile."

To bow to the Buddha is easy; a reverent heart is hard. If the mind is not devout, all is idle; the five limbs (the two hands, the two knees and the head) hanging in emptiness (with no reverent heart) is strength spent for nothing—though the skull (this heartless husk) be knocked to pieces, it is futile.
If one bows to the Buddha while thinking of other things (indulging in idle thoughts), then there is no reverent heart and

To recite the sutras is easy; to understand them is hard. To chant with the mouth without understanding, all is idle; to understand but not to put into practice is strength spent for nothing—though one chant ten thousand scrolls a day, it is futile.

[Great awakening] Concerning Master Hanshan's great awakening at the age of thirty, the Dream-Wanderings Collection

Autobiographical Chronicle of the Old Man Hanshan, records: I dwelt alone at Longmen on the north terrace of Mount Wutai, holding to a single thought. When people came, I did not open my mouth to speak but only looked at them.

One day after the morning gruel, while walking in meditation, I suddenly stood still and entered samādhi. Body and mind vanished, and there remained only a great treasury of radiance, perfect and utterly still, like a great perfect mirror, in which mountains, rivers and the great earth all appeared as reflections. When I came out of samādhi, my mind opened as though a thatch had been pulled away, and I sought my own body and mind and could not find them at all. Then I spoke a verse: "Suddenly the mad mind's single thought is stilled; / within and without, faculties and dusts are wholly clear; / I turn and break through the vast empty space; / the myriad forms in dense array may rise and cease at will (let the myriad forms rise and cease as they will, while the mind remains unmoved)." From that time on, within and without were still and serene, and the hindrances of sound, form and appearance came no more; where formerly I had been baffled by doubt, I was now instantly and clearly enlightened. When I returned to my thatched hut, I saw that the pot in which I cooked my rice was covered with dust; since I lived alone, I did not know how many days had passed in samādhi.

[Movement and stillness as one] According to the Autobiographical Chronicle of the Old Man Hanshan: at the age of thirty-two, Master Hanshan made a vow to write out one complete copy of the Great Expansive Buddha Flower Adornment Sutra in blood and gold (drawing his own blood and mixing it with gold powder). When Empress Dowager Li learned of this, she granted him gold paper for writing the sutra. In the fourth month of the following year, Master Hanshan began to write. As he wrote, no matter whether the stroke was a dot or a line, at every touch of the brush his mind recited the Buddha's name once. Monks and laypeople wandering on the mountain who came to the Master's quiet room would invariably exchange greetings and ask for instruction, and the Master answered them while his hand never stopped copying.

; the Master would invite them to sit on the meditation couch and talk of the Dharma with them, while his hand still never stopped writing. So it was every day: though people came and went and he received them and conversed, his writing of the sutra never ceased, and in his mind not the slightest movement could be found. Many old worthies (senior, deeply learned men) heard of the Master's

circumstances and found them hard to believe. One day the old worthies brought many of their disciples to the Master's quiet room, wanting to verify exactly what was going on. Beside the Master they deliberately asked questions and made an uproar, using every means to disturb him; then, when the Master had finished writing a section,

took it and compared it with the original text, and truly there was not the slightest error. Only then were they convinced that the Master's skill was far from ordinary. Yet they still did not understand it, and went to ask Master Miaofeng: "Why is Master Hanshan able to use one mind for many things at once?" Master Miaofeng answered: "My elder Dharma brother's Buddha-recitation samādhi has reached utter purity!"

[Twenty years passed, and he sat upright as in life; thereupon his body was lacquered with gold and raised to the seat] After Master Hanshan's parinirvana, his countenance was still as pure and smooth as jade, his lips still as red and moist, his hands and feet still as soft as ever, just as when he used to enter samādhi. After his disciples escorted the Master's flesh body to Mount Lu, because the climate of Mount Lu was damp and overcast, his attendant Fushan built a stupa court and enshrined the Master's flesh-body casket on the stupa. Twenty years later, the disciples of Lingnan went to Mount Lu to welcome the Master back to Caoxi. When they arrived at Caoxi, the disciples who guarded the casket, Guangcheng and Cili, saw that the casket had a crack (xia
a fissure), and they secretly bored a small
hole in the crack to look
inside; they saw the Master's flesh body sitting upright as in life,
they opened the casket chamber and saw the Master sitting cross-legged and upright, as majestic as in life, his nails and hair still growing, his complexion still

, and the purple silk robe and the strings of beads still new. Just then a wind blew up, and the garments suddenly scattered like clouds and stars, fluttering away with the wind; the local people gathered them up as auspicious tokens.

At that very moment a monk suddenly appeared and asked to use the Indian method (of ancient India) to protect the Master's flesh body. Having obtained the assembly's consent, he smeared the Master's body with sandalwood powder from Hainan, like lacquer. When the monk had finished, he simply went away.

While the Master was alive, a devout woman of Caoxi made a vow to embroider a robe of a thousand Buddhas to offer to the Master; fearing that her breath would defile it, she covered her mouth with yellow silk as she embroidered
By the time the thousand-Buddha robe was finished, the Master had already

and been placed in the casket, and the robe was stored away in the treasury chests of Baolin Monastery. Now this robe was brought out again and draped over the Master's flesh body; though twenty years had passed, it shone with a radiance as if newly made. When the sealing of the casket was complete, the disciples enshrined the Master in the old stupa court and changed its name to Hanshan Temple, about half a li from Nanhua Monastery, where the flesh body of the Sixth Patriarch rests. Following the custom of making offerings to the Sixth Patriarch, the disciples each morning used a bowl of hot fragrant water to steam the Master's face until it perspired, then wiped it dry with a towel, and afterward, just as in life, offered him food and drink. Once a year they also bathed him. (Excerpted from
